analysis.one_liner: Bans oil and gas seismic airgun blasting surveys along the Atlantic coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit geological and geophysical activities — mainly deep-penetration seismic airgun surveys, plus test drilling and electromagnetic surveys — done in support of oil, gas, or methane hydrate exploration in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2] [S3]. Seismic airgun surveys fire loud airgun pulses at the ocean floor to map oil and gas deposits; the bill would make it illegal for any person or federal agency to conduct them for fossil fuel exploration in those Atlantic waters [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA) with Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ) and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, beach communities, and coastal businesses along the Atlantic seaboard would be spared the noise disruption and environmental risk that seismic airgun surveys bring; commercial and recreational fishing interests and marine wildlife would avoid the acoustic impacts; and the Atlantic coast would remain off-limits to the first step of offshore drilling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal communities and marine life

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits conducting geological or geophysical activities in support of oil, gas, or methane hydrate exploration or development anywhere in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, or Straits of Florida planning areas of the outer Continental Shelf [S2] [S3].

The covered activities are defined to include the survey methods described in the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's 2014 programmatic environmental impact statement, which cover deep-penetration seismic airgun surveys, electromagnetic surveys, and stratigraphic and shallow test drilling [S2].
The ban applies to any person or any agency of the United States, so neither companies nor federal agencies could run these surveys in the affected Atlantic waters [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and the seismic survey contractors they hire would lose access to Atlantic offshore acreage for exploration, and any future development that exploration would have supported would not move forward. Energy consumers could, in principle, see slightly tighter supply from foreclosed offshore resources, though Atlantic drilling was not commercially producing.

drawbacks.text: The bill forecloses exploration for domestic oil and gas resources on the Atlantic outer Continental Shelf, reducing the country's knowledge of and potential access to those energy resources [S2].

The ban is categorical: it applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' and covers all oil-, gas-, and methane-hydrate-related geophysical work in four vast planning areas, leaving no pathway for even narrowly tailored surveys [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades potential future Atlantic oil and gas development for protection of coastal waters from seismic surveying. The economic cost is speculative, since Atlantic offshore exploration had not advanced to production, while the benefits fall on fishing, tourism, and coastal communities that live with the direct effects of airgun noise. The main design weakness is that it is an absolute ban with no exception process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and died there without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA) introduced the bill on March 7, 2019, joined as an original cosponsor by Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ), a Republican from New Jersey [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction; the committee never took it up [S5].
On March 28, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it remained for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 13 cosponsors, 12 of them Democrats and 1 a Republican, and no further floor or committee action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies and seismic survey contractors are better off in the sense that Atlantic waters remain open under existing law for future exploration, since nothing stood in the bill's way except a committee that never acted. No one else gained anything from the bill's death.

industries.note: The bill would bar the seismic surveys that are the first step toward drilling in the Atlantic, foreclosing exploration of the outer Continental Shelf there. Its interest ran against the coastal communities and marine resources the ban protects.
Specialty firms that run airgun and electromagnetic surveys for oil and gas companies would lose a prospective Atlantic market entirely under the ban.

Fishing interests depend on marine ecosystems that airgun blasting can disrupt, so the survey ban protects their resource. They are an industry benefitting alongside the public rather than bearing a cost.
